## Overview

TWAS weights are per-variant coefficients that predict a molecular
phenotype (gene expression, splicing, protein abundance) from genotype.
Once learned, the weights are combined with GWAS summary statistics to
compute per-gene TWAS Z-scores (covered in the
[TWAS Z-score + causal inference vignette](twas-zscore.html)).

`twasWeightsPipeline()` is a single that accepts multiple input types. The
output is always a `TwasWeights` collection (a `GRangesList` subclass keyed
by `(study, context, trait, method)`, one element per tuple).

| Input class | Methods supported |
|---|---|
| `QtlDataset` | Univariate: LASSO, elastic net, ridge, mr.ash, MCP, SCAD, L0Learn, Bayesian alphabet, DPR. Multivariate: mr.mash, mvsusie |
| `MultiStudyQtlDataset` | Iterates over embedded studies; same methods as `QtlDataset` |
| `QtlSumStats` | RSS-only: LASSO, elastic net, ridge, mr.ash, MCP, SCAD, L0Learn, DPR, PRS-CS, P+T. Multivariate: mr.mash, mvsusie |

```{r load-packages}
library(pecotmr)
```

## Bundled inputs

```{r bundled}
data(qtlDatasetExample, qtlSumStatsExample, multiStudyQtlDatasetExample)
```

## Individual-level weights

The simplest individual-level call learns a single regression-based weight set
from a `QtlDataset`. Cross-validation is off by default
(`CrossValidationParam(folds = 0)`).
Like `fineMappingPipeline()`, you need to tell it which genotype window to
extract — `cisWindow` (per trait) is the most common choice.

Fine-mapping methods (`susie`, `susieInf`, `susieAsh`, `mvsusie`, `fsusie`) are
not re-fit by `twasWeightsPipeline()` - instead run fine-mapping models with
`fineMappingPipeline()` first and pass the result via `fineMappingResult = …`
(see the next section).

```{r individual-quickstart}
tw <- twasWeightsPipeline(qtlDatasetExample, methods = "lasso", cisWindow = 1e6)
tw
```

Extract the per-variant weights for one tuple:

```{r individual-weights}
entry <- twasWeights(
    tw,
    studyName = "study1",
    context = "brain",
    trait = "ENSG_example",
    method = "lasso"
)
head(weights(entry))
```

CV performance:

```{r individual-cv}
cvResult(entry)
```

The entry's `variantIds` slot lists the LD-aligned variant set the
weights are defined on:

```{r individual-vids}
length(variantIds(entry))
```

## Including a fine-mapping susie fit in the TWAS ensemble

The posterior effect estimates of SuSiE fine-mapping models are themselves a
set of per-variant weight estimates. When you pass an existing
`QtlFineMappingResult` to `twasWeightsPipeline()`, the trimmed susie fit for
each matching `(study, context, trait)` tuple is added to the ensemble as an
additional weights row instead of being re-fit.

The same holds under cross-validation: each fold needs a fit trained on that
fold's rows, and the weights pipeline will not produce one. Run the
fine-mapping with `crossValidationParam` so those per-fold fits travel with the
result —
requesting a fine-mapping method under cross-validation without them is an
error. That fold partition then governs the whole run: every other weight
method is cross-validated on the same folds, which is what makes their
scores comparable. The fold samples must be the samples of the dataset being
scored, or the run stops rather than scoring a fit against rows it was never
separated from.

```{r individual-with-fmr}
fmr <- fineMappingPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "susie",
    cisWindow = 1e6,
    crossValidationParam = CrossValidationParam(folds = 3)
)
tw2 <- twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = c("susie", "lasso"),
    cisWindow = 1e6,
    fineMappingResult = fmr
)
```

## Multi-study weights

```{r multistudy}
msTw <- twasWeightsPipeline(
    multiStudyQtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "lasso",
    cisWindow = 1e6
)
table(msTw$study)
```

The call for iterating over the studies of a MultiStudyQtlDataset is identical
to the call for a single QtlDataset.

## Multiple weight methods at once

Pass a character vector to fit several methods on the same fold split and
return them as separate `(method)` rows in the collection. Fine-mapping methods
(`susie`, `susieInf`, `susieAsh`, `mvsusie`) can only be included if their
results are present in the object passed to the `fineMappingResult` argument:

```{r multimethod, eval=FALSE}
# TWAS-regression only — no fineMappingResult needed.
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = c("lasso", "enet", "ridge", "mrash")
)

# Add a fine-mapping susie row by providing the QtlFineMappingResult.
fmr <- fineMappingPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "susie",
    cisWindow = 1e6
)
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = c("susie", "lasso", "enet", "ridge", "mrash"),
    cisWindow = 1e6,
    fineMappingResult = fmr
)
```

## RSS / sumstats weights

```{r sumstats}
twSs <- twasWeightsPipeline(qtlSumStatsExample, methods = "lasso")
twSs
```

The RSS path computes LD as needed from each row's LD reference in the
`QtlSumStats` collection. The same rule holds for
fine-mapping methods here: they are not re-fit, so run
`fineMappingPipeline()` on the `QtlSumStats` first and pass its result as
`fineMappingResult`.

## Multivariate (multi-context) weights

When you have multiple contexts for the same trait (e.g. multi-tissue
expression), pass `methods = "mrmash"` to do a joint multivariate fit:

```{r multivariate, eval=FALSE}
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "mrmash",
    contexts = c("brain", "liver")
)
```

To choose the axes yourself, pass a `jointSpecification`: a character
vector of axes, or `list(axes = , scope = )` to limit the fit to listed
studies, contexts or traits. The `jointSpecification` argument in
`?twasWeightsPipeline` gives the full grammar. On a `QtlSumStats` the
contexts are fitted against one LD matrix, so their rows must share an LD
reference.

```{r joint, eval=FALSE}
# `qd`: a QtlDataset whose traits are measured in brain, liver and more.
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qd,
    methods = "mrmash",
    jointSpecification = list(list(
        axes = "context",
        scope = list(context = c("brain", "liver"))
    ))
)
```

## Calling a weight method directly

Each `methods =` value dispatches to an exported function, and those
functions are usable on their own. Reach for one when you want to fit a
single model to a matrix you already have — tuning a penalty, comparing
methods outside the pipeline, or debugging a method that behaves oddly on
your data.

The individual-level methods take `X` (genotypes) and `y` (phenotype) and
return a weight vector:

```{r direct-method}
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
p <- 30
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("v", 1:p)))
y <- as.vector(X %*% c(rep(0.4, 3), rep(0, p - 3)) + rnorm(n))

w <- lassoWeights(X = X, y = y)
c(length = length(w), nonzero = sum(w != 0))
```

The families, and the `methods =` name each answers to:

| Family | `methods =` | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Penalized regression | `lasso`, `enet`, `ridge`, `mcp`, `scad`, `l0learn` | `lassoWeights()`, `enetWeights()`, `ridgeWeights()`, … |
| Bayesian alphabet | `bayesA` … `bayesR`, `bLasso` | `bayesAWeights()`, `bLassoWeights()`, … |
| Dirichlet process regression | `dprVb`, `dprGibbs`, `dprAdaptiveGibbs` | `dprVbWeights()`, `dprGibbsWeights()`, … |
| PRS-CS | `prsCs` (sumstats input only) | `prsCsWeights()` |
| mr.mash / mr.ash | `mrmash`, `mrash` | `mrmashWeights()`, `mrashWeights()` |
| SuSiE family | `susie`, `susieInf`, `susieAsh`, `mvsusie`, `fsusie` | `susieWeights()`, `mvsusieWeights()`, … |

Every token is camelCase, matching the function names. Snake_case spellings
are not accepted: `bayes_r`, `dpr_vb` and `susie_inf` all error with the list
of known tokens.

Most families have an RSS counterpart taking summary statistics and an LD
reference instead of `X`/`y` — `lassosumRssWeights()` for `lasso`,
`enetRssWeights()` and `ridgeRssWeights()` for `enet` and `ridge`,
`mcpRssWeights()`, `sdprWeights()` (SDPR) for `dprGibbs`, `susieRssWeights()`,
and so on; the Bayesian alphabet, `dprVb` and `dprAdaptiveGibbs` have none.
`enet` mixes the lasso and ridge penalties at `alpha = 0.5` on either input;
`methods = list(enet = list(alpha = 0.3))` sets another mixing. Those are what `twasWeightsPipeline()` calls when the input is a
`QtlSumStats`. The LD
reference is the same `ldReference` the rest of the package takes: a
genotype panel from `readGenotypes()`, a `GenotypeMixture` or an
`LdMatrix`, matched to the statistics by their `variantNames`. lassosum,
the penalized methods, PRS-CS and SDPR use a genotype reference through its
standardized genotypes without forming the LD matrix; the mr.ash and
mr.mash engines take the matrix, which is formed over the statistics'
variants.

Several of these engines estimate more than the weights, and
`fitRetention = "slim"` keeps it as the `"fit"` attribute of the weights they
return: SDPR's heritability estimate (`h2`), PRS-CS's posterior shrinkage
parameters (`psiEst`, `sigmaEst`, `phiEst`), and for lassosum and the
penalized methods the search itself --- `path` has one row per LD shrinkage
`s` and penalty `lambda`, with the objective (`fbeta`), `loss`, convergence
flag and number of non-zero weights, and marks the candidate returned.
`fitRetention = "full"` adds each candidate's coefficients.

```{r rss-fit}
# An LdMatrix is keyed by chrom:pos:A2:A1 variant ids.
ids <- sprintf("chr1:%d:A:G", 100L * seq_len(p))
R <- cor(X)
dimnames(R) <- list(ids, ids)
stat <- list(
    z = as.vector(cor(X, y)) * sqrt(n),
    n = rep(n, p),
    variantNames = ids
)
w <- lassosumRssWeights(stat, LdMatrix(R), fitRetention = "slim")
head(attr(w, "fit")$path)
```

The mr.mash methods need prior covariance matrices, built by
`buildMrmashPriorMatrices()`. Pass `dataDrivenPriorMatrices` to add
data-driven components alongside the canonical mixture --- `computeCovDiag()`
gives the per-condition diagonal, and `mashr::cov_flash()` returns a list of
FLASH-derived components in the shape that argument expects.

## Cross-validation, ensembling and prediction

The pipeline's `ensemble` method is not a model of its own — it is a weighted
combination of the others, with the weights chosen by cross-validation.
Those steps are exported too:

- `twasWeightsCv()` runs the cross-validation that scores each method.
- `learnTwasWeights()` runs the requested weight methods on the full data.
- `combineTwasWeights()` forms the ensemble from per-method weights.
- `estimateSparsity()` reports how sparse a fitted weight vector is.

Once you have weights, `twasPredict()` applies them to a genotype matrix.
It takes a *named list* of weight vectors, with names ending in `_weights`,
and returns one predicted column per entry:

```{r predict}
pred <- twasPredict(X, list(gene1_weights = w))
names(pred)
round(cor(as.vector(pred[[1]]), y), 3)
```

That correlation is the in-sample prediction accuracy — on real data you
would want the cross-validated version from `twasWeightsCv()` instead, since
in-sample accuracy is optimistic by construction.

## Common parameters

```{r tw-params, eval=FALSE}
twasWeightsPipeline(
    qtlDatasetExample,
    methods = "susie",
    contexts = "brain",
    traitId = "ENSG_example",
    cisWindow = 5e5,
    # or, in place of traitId + cisWindow, a literal window:
    # region = GenomicRanges::GRanges("chr22:25000000-26000000"),
    crossValidationParam = CrossValidationParam(
        folds = 5,
        BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam(),
        samplePartition = NULL,
        maxVariants = -1
    ),
    # required for a fine-mapping method, and under folds > 1 it must carry
    # the per-fold fits (fineMappingPipeline(..., crossValidationParam = ...))
    fineMappingResult = fmr,
    ensembleParam = EnsembleParam(
        enabled = TRUE,
        r2Threshold = 0.01,
        solver = "quadprog"
    ),
    estimatePi = TRUE,
    residualizationParam = ResidualizationParam(
        phenotypeCovariates = NULL,
        genotypeCovariates = NULL
    ),
    weightsDataType = NULL,
    phenotypeFilterParam = PhenotypeFilterParam(naAction = "drop")
)
```

-  `EnsembleParam(enabled = TRUE)` adds an additional `ensembleWeights` row to
    the collection — a weighted combination of the individual methods' CV
    predictions, filtered by that bundle's `r2Threshold`.
-  `phenotypeFilterParam` is the run's phenotype QC (see the
    [fine-mapping vignette](fine-mapping.html#common-parameters) for
    semantics).

## Reading the result

`TwasWeights` is a `GRangesList` subclass keyed by the 4-tuple
`(study, context, trait, method)` — one element per tuple, holding the
variants its weights are aligned to. The tuple and the per-tuple payloads are
`mcols()` columns, reached with `$`:

```{r tw-shape}
tw
colnames(tw)
tw$method
```

`as.data.frame()` gives the long per-variant view across every method at once,
which is usually what you want for inspection:

```{r tw-table}
head(as.data.frame(tw), 3)
```

To pull one method's weights, pass the tuple to the accessor:

```{r tw-one-tuple}
key <- list(
    studyName = tw$study[[1L]],
    context = tw$context[[1L]],
    trait = tw$trait[[1L]],
    method = tw$method[[1L]]
)
w <- do.call(weights, c(list(tw), key))
length(w)
do.call(weightStandardized, c(list(tw), key)) # TRUE from the pipeline
do.call(weightsDataType, c(list(tw), key)) # tag carried through for reporting
```

`weightStandardized()` is `TRUE` for anything the pipeline fitted: genotypes
are centred and scaled to unit variance before every method runs, so all the
weights are on one scale. That scaling is part of residualization —
`ResidualizationParam(scaleResiduals = FALSE)` opts out, and it is on by
default — so the
recorded flag reports what was done rather than what you claimed. That is not bookkeeping. Every method here returns
coefficients on the scale of the `X` it was handed — exactly so for glmnet,
ncvreg, L0Learn, mr.ash, the Bayesian alphabet and `susieWeights()` — while
the DPR samplers are not even scale-equivariant, so rescaling `X` changes
their fit rather than just its units. Standardizing up front removes the
question, and lands on the scale the LD correlations and z-scores behind a
TWAS Z already use. `learnTwasWeights()` still takes `weightStandardized`,
because there you supply `X` yourself.

`weights()` returns a named numeric vector for univariate methods and a
matrix for multivariate ones. The remaining payloads are keyed the same way:
`variantIds()` for the aligned variant set, `cvResult()` for the
cross-validation record (`rsq`, `r`, predicted values), and `methodFits()` for
the full fit object when the pipeline kept fits (`fitRetention != "none"`).
`resolveWeights()` returns the weights and their variant IDs together, which
is the form the downstream TWAS and MR steps consume.

## Publishing the weights

The same two writers that write fine-mapping results write weights.
`writeGwasVcf()` writes a GWAS-VCF-style file: one record per variant, one
sample per fitted model, the weight in the `WGT` FORMAT field, and each
model's identity in its own `##SAMPLE` header line. `writeBed()` writes the
same thing as a long table, one row per (variant, model).

```{r tw-write, eval=FALSE}
writeGwasVcf(tw, "weights.vcf.gz")
writeGwasVcf(tw, "lasso_weights.vcf.gz", method = "lasso") # one model
writeBed(tw, "weights.bed.gz")
```

Both export the **full-data fit only**, and refuse an object that has none —
`crossValidationParam = CrossValidationParam(fitFullData = FALSE)` produces rows
holding nothing but cross-validation results, and those cannot be published:
they describe held-out folds, and fold membership is sample-level information.
For the same reason neither exporter writes CV metrics. Those stay on the
object:

```{r tw-cv, eval=FALSE}
cv <- cvResult(tw, studyName = "s1", context = "brain", trait = "g1",
               method = "susie")
cv$performance # per-method metric matrix: corr, rsq, adj_rsq, pval, RMSE, MAE
```

Fine-mapping-derived rows (`susie`, `susie_inf`, `susie_ash`, `mvsusie`,
`fsusie`) are skipped with a message by **both** exporters, because their
"weights" are the fine-mapping posterior re-expressed — export the
fine-mapping result instead, which carries the posterior, its standard error
and the credible sets. Selecting only such a method, as in
`method = "susie"`, is therefore an error rather than an empty file.

`readTwasWeights()` reads either format back into a `TwasWeights`:

```{r tw-read, eval=FALSE}
tw <- readTwasWeights("weights.bed.gz")
tw <- readTwasWeights(
    "weights.bed.gz",
    which = GenomicRanges::GRanges("chr22:10000000-19000000")
)
```

A weight is all it requires, so a table converted from another tool reads with
nothing but variant ids and a `WGT` column — plus the identity axes the
collection is keyed by, which `studyName` / `context` / `trait` / `method`
supply when the file does not record them. `weightStandardized` is required
when the file does not say which genotype scale the weights are on: that is
not recoverable from the numbers, since converting between the two rescales
every variant by its own allele-frequency-dependent factor.
